research: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sting — 1936 Depression setting; the con is 'the wire', a fake off-track betting parlour (a 'big store'); the final switcheroo is a staged FBI raid and fake shooting that the mark (and the audience) believe is real, so the mark leaves never knowing he was taken; muted browns and maroons, 1930s-style lighting, period costume; sections opened by painted magazine-style title cards; ragtime score.
https://reelviews.net/reelviews/sting-the — the film is structured by chapter title cards naming the stages of a con; the audience is let into the con, then is itself fooled at the end.
https://catalog.afi.com/Catalog/moviedetails/54391 — production record for the 1973 film (period design, title cards, ragtime adaptation).
https://thedispatch.com/?p=48611 — why the big con still plays: the audience is a second mark, misdirected along with the villain.
https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Confidence_game — short con vs big con; the big store; the pigeon drop (mark puts up money to share a 'find').
https://spyscape.com/article/spyscapes-glossary-of-con-artist-slang — con slang: the mark, the big store, the wire.
https://EN.wikipedia.com/wiki/Shell_game — the shell game is a rigged choice: sleight of hand means the mark loses whichever shell he picks; the model for our 'two envelopes, same contents'.
https://tropedia.fandom.com/wiki/Satchel_Switcheroo — the switcheroo as a screen device: identical containers swapped so the audience loses track of which holds what.

https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/ultimate-prompting-guide-for-nano-banana — narrative prompts (subject, action, place, composition, style), positive framing, name lens/film stock/lighting, put on-image text in quotes and describe its lettering; 9:16 supported.
https://runware.ai/docs/models/google-nano-banana-2/guides/prompting — camera angle and depth language (low angle, overhead, shallow focus) steers composition.
notes: The con: a 1930s 'wire store' where the race is an election with two runners at even odds. The voter is the mark and plays it straight; the joke is on the house. The switcheroo is a shell game: under the counter both envelopes hold the same arms order (ORDER No. 0417) and sit on a drawer of freshly printed money, so the deal goes through whichever he picks. In the film the audience is conned along with the mark; here BadCode is the one who sees the switch and, in S4, rips back the curtain and catches the con men (blue tie and red tie) mid-handshake: the decision-makers are named by the stamps, never the viewer. Timing ~15 s: S1 0:00-0:03, S2 0:03-0:07, S3 0:07-0:11, S4 0:11-0:16 carrying the spoken closing line. Look b carries invented chapter titles (THE COUNTER / THE PICK / THE SWITCH / THE PAY-OFF), deliberately not the film's card wording; its S4 puts a short slice of the line on screen; the editor should add the full line as a caption on a/c if wanted. Look c keeps only the stamp ink in colour: both stamps in the same red, a quiet hint that they are one stamp. Music, if any, should be invented period piano, not Joplin or the film's score. No faces are shown on the suited men; check every take for legible stamp text and redo any where a stamp is misspelt.

beats.name: S1. The set-up
beats.blurb: A 1930s backstreet 'betting parlour' where the race has two runners: the dealer fans two envelopes, APPROVED BY THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY and APPROVED BY THE LABOUR PARTY, at even odds.

beats.name: S2. The pick
beats.blurb: The working man, the mark, chooses one envelope in good faith; the dealer plays the fair host.

beats.name: S3. The switch
beats.blurb: Under the counter both envelopes are opened: the same arms order, same number, comes out of each, next to a drawer of freshly printed money. The choice was rigged both ways.

beats.name: S4. The sting
beats.blurb: BadCode rips back the curtain and catches the house: blue tie and red tie shaking hands over the stamped rifle crate and the new money. Spoken (and optionally on screen): "They're going to print the money and the weapon sales will still happen anyway, everything else is a distraction."

looks.a: Photographic period film still: 1930s backstreet betting parlour, 35mm film grain, muted browns, maroons and tobacco gold, warm tungsten practicals, 40mm lens, faces kept out of frame or under hat brims.
looks.b: Painted chapter-card illustration: opaque gouache 1930s magazine-cover style, flat poster colour, visible brush strokes, an invented hand-lettered chapter title at the top of every frame (THE COUNTER, THE PICK, THE SWITCH, THE PAY-OFF). Invented art, not the film's.
looks.c: Press-flash evidence photo: harsh single flashbulb from the camera, high-contrast black-and-white silver gelatin print, deep black falloff, the ONLY colour in the frame is the red ink of the two stamps, like a 1930s tabloid crime photograph.

stills.prompt: Vertical 9:16 period film still. A cramped 1930s backstreet betting parlour: dark oak counter, brass lamp, a chalkboard behind reading "TODAY: TWO RUNNERS. ODDS EVENS / EVENS". A dealer in a pinstripe waistcoat and sleeve garters, face hidden under a trilby brim, fans two cream envelopes across the counter toward camera. Each carries a crisp rubber stamp in red ink, legible: "APPROVED BY THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY" and "APPROVED BY THE LABOUR PARTY". Shot on 35mm film with a 40mm lens, shallow focus on the envelopes, warm tungsten light, cigarette haze, muted browns and maroons, real grain. Thanks.

At the top, invented hand-lettered chapter title "THE COUNTER" in cream serif capitals. Below, a slick dealer in a pinstripe waistcoat, face shaded by his hat brim, leans over a polished counter and fans out two envelopes like playing cards. Their stamps are painted clearly and legibly: "APPROVED BY THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY" and "APPROVED BY THE LABOUR PARTY". Ochre, maroon and bottle-green palette, warm lamplight. Thanks.

Hidden under the counter, the dealer's hands slit both envelopes, stamped "APPROVED BY THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY" and "APPROVED BY THE LABOUR PARTY", and the same typed sheet slides out of each: an arms export order, identical, both headed "ORDER No. 0417". Below them an open drawer packed with crisp freshly printed banknotes of an invented design. Narrow slice of tungsten light, 35mm grain, muted browns and maroons, 28mm lens. Thanks.

A cutaway view of the counter like a stage trick: above, the man chooses; below, hidden, a single double-headed rubber stamp printing "APPROVED BY THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY" on one end and "APPROVED BY THE LABOUR PARTY" on the other, and both envelopes feeding into one wooden crate stencilled "ORDER No. 0417". Beside each lies its contents: two identical typed arms export orders, both "ORDER No. 0417", same signature, same carbon smudge, plus a band-wrapped brick of new banknotes of invented design. Vertical 9:16 period film still. A back-room curtain is ripped aside by a figure in a black balaclava. The balaclava has no eye, nose or mouth holes, so no skin shows anywhere; a large white ring is stitched round the whole face, and one small red triangle with rounded corners, pointing down, sits high inside the ring on the right-hand side of the picture. Gloves on both hands; no robot parts. Revealed: two men in suits, one blue tie and one red tie, faces turned away, shaking hands over a crate of rifles stamped "APPROVED BY THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY" and "APPROVED BY THE LABOUR PARTY", stacks of fresh invented banknotes beside them. 35mm grain, tungsten light, muted browns and maroons. Thanks.
